moves.spoken: Our first 2000-rated opponent — and I'll play the c3 Sicilian, the Alapin, which I've recommended in this rating range for a while.
He plays d6, which isn't the best line against it — it lets us take control of the centre.
He hits the e4-pawn, so we defend it with the bishop to d3 — and there are subtleties to watch for, particularly if he plays the knight to c6.
The knight to f3 defends d4. His bishop to g4 here would look intimidating...
...but instead he plays the very passive e6.
Two ways to continue here: open the centre with dxc5, which makes a lot of sense, or play flexibly with the bishop to g5.

Let's develop by the book — the knight to d2. That's the downside of the Alapin: you can't route this knight to c3. But it's fine here, and it buttresses the e4-pawn. We're clearly better, with a nice pawn centre.
He plays e5. Now a lot of people struggle with the decision between capturing and pushing.
Taking on e5 would open the position to his benefit and let him attack our bishop — so d5, keeping the centre closed. Our space advantage should, in theory, tell against him.
There's a tactical detail here I failed to anticipate — let's see if he finds it.
He does — the knight takes on d5. I'd missed this move.
But that's the beauty of being positionally better — you can blunder a pawn and still be fine. He's opened the d-file, so the question is how to pressure the pawn on d6.
The knight to c4 — no disaster, still a good position, but I did just make an instructive mistake.
We win the pawn back on d6; roughly equal. And if he pushes d5, we take, and his e5-pawn hangs — we're eyeing that pawn too.
His knight on b4 is a nice counterweight. His best was the queen to b6, preparing a rook to d8; the queen to c7 is not the most accurate.

The knight on d6 is our vulnerable piece — so rather than use the get-out-of-jail rook to c1 to activate the rook, we evacuate the knight to b5. Chess is all about priorities, and the top priority is getting that knight out.
Now our knight is safely out and defended — something we couldn't do a move ago.
He's forgotten the pawn is hanging — the knight takes on e5, and we're up a pawn. Sometimes chess is about resisting the by-the-book move and prioritising.
If he grabs on a2 he'll lose material.
We retreat the knight to c3 — an even safer square.

The rook to d8 — and we must be careful, because the queen to e1 walks into a fork. So the queen goes to a4 instead, active and pressuring his knights. When he tries the queen to c5 it doesn't actually attack our knight, because his knight on b4 would hang. That b4-knight is what cramps us, so e3 compels the trade — and with us a pawn up, trades are good, plus it removes his strongest piece. Then the finishing trick: with his queen in contact with the rook, we swing a rook to d8, and he can't defend it without a back-rank mate or giving up the rook; the queen to f5 finishes with mate to follow.
A quick recap: he played d6, which handed us central control — a line I've even played from the Black side.

When his bishop pins from g4 and the long diagonal opens, the knight takes on e5 becomes possible — we're not blundering the queen, we're setting up a combination: the check on b5 in between wins the queen back, and when the smoke clears we're up a piece. It's the same idea as the famous Queen's Gambit knight-to-d7 trap.

My key mistake was developing the bishop to g5 — it became a big liability. Better to just take, play the queen to e2, and put a rook on d1 to x-ray his queen, maybe even e5 to cement the centre. This bishop-to-g5 setup, facing off with his dark-squared bishop, gets into trouble precisely because of the knight takes on d5 — that same knight then defends the bishop. Taking on f6 was possible, but it hands Black the two bishops and a later f5 break.
